name: Raw carrot salad (Ray Peat)
lead: The raw carrot salad is a daily food habit associated with the bioenergetic diet popularised by the American biologist Ray Peat. It is a grated or shredded raw carrot dressed with a little oil, vinegar and salt, eaten as a side dish. Followers describe it as a gut-and-hormone routine that they connect to clearer skin, less bloating and a leaner, less puffy look.[1][2]

In Peat's account as relayed by his followers, raw carrot fibre stimulates the intestine and binds estrogen that the liver sends into bile, so less is reabsorbed, while the vinegar and oil dressing suppresses bacterial growth and lowers endotoxin absorption. One widely quoted line says raw carrots, by stimulating the intestine, often help lower estrogen and raise progesterone.[1] Followers link lower gut endotoxin and estrogen to better skin, hair and body composition. Carrots also supply beta-carotene, which can warm skin tone when carotenoid intake is high.

Dietary research on fibre and estrogen exists, but no published human trial has tested the carrot salad itself.[2] The salad became widely shared as a recipe on wellness blogs and social media, usually under the label of hormone balance.[2]

chain: Fibre and carotenoids reach the gut and skin
Clearer, warmer-looking complexion as described by followers
angle.text: Followers eat a shredded raw carrot with oil and vinegar each day, reasoning that it supports gut and hormone balance and in turn skin clarity and a leaner look. Carotenoid-rich foods are also discussed for a warmer skin tone.

infobox: Shredded raw carrot, oil, vinegar, salt

paras: The salad is a small portion of raw carrot, often grated or cut into thin strips, dressed with a modest amount of oil (coconut or olive oil are commonly named), a splash of vinegar and some salt. Peat-diet communities treat it as a staple alongside foods such as orange juice, milk and cooked mushrooms.

According to a 2012 post quoting Peat, the claim has several parts: fibre reduces absorption of bacterial toxins from the intestine, the vinegar and oil dressing adds to this by suppressing bacterial growth, fibre binds estrogen carried in bile so less is reabsorbed, and lower bacterial fermentation is linked to lower intestinal serotonin.[1] The same post says Peat discussed vitamin A separately and noted that excess carotene may inhibit progesterone synthesis, and that the post draws on older writings that may not reflect his later views.[1]

sections.h: Related research on fibre and estrogen
paras: The underlying biology that the liver tags estrogen for removal and gut bacteria can strip the tag so it is reabsorbed is established. A review article on the salad cites a 1982 observational study in which vegetarian women had more fibre intake, larger stool output and more estrogen in faeces, a 1997 study of 62 premenopausal women in which wheat bran lowered estrone and estradiol while oat and corn bran did not, and a study in which speeding bowel transit reduced several estrogen measures.[2] It adds that olive oil improved carotenoid absorption from carrots in a digestion study. None of these tested the salad or measured estrogen after eating it.[2]

Proponents say the fibre in raw carrot binds or speeds clearance of estrogen and gut endotoxin, reducing what they regard as a drag on thyroid function and skin quality.[1] Users report smoother skin, less bloating and a sharper facial outline.

On looksmax.org, Ray Peat's diet is discussed in threads including a resource list on metabolic rate and hormones, one on his view of sodium and water retention, and members' notes on the diet.[3][4][5]

No studies found on the carrot salad as Peat's followers describe it. General research on dietary fibre and estrogen excretion exists, and the studies described above were of broader categories; the Frondescent article states that no published human trial shows the salad lowers estrogen or removes endotoxin.[2]
Very high carotenoid intake can give the skin a yellow-orange tint (carotenemia), which is harmless and fades when intake falls. Raw fibre can cause gas or loose stools in people unaccustomed to it.

lore.intro: The carrot salad is mentioned in Peat-influenced communities as a daily staple, and looksmax.org members discuss Peat's diet for hormones and water retention.[3][4]

claims.claim: A daily raw carrot lowers estrogen and raises progesterone.
claims.believers: Peat is quoted as saying raw carrots, by stimulating the intestine, often help lower estrogen and raise progesterone.[1]
claims.experts: Small human studies show that some fibre types and faster transit change estrogen measures, but no trial has tested the salad.[2]

claims.claim: The carrot salad lowers gut endotoxin.
claims.believers: Followers say fibre plus vinegar and oil suppress gut bacteria and reduce toxin absorption.[1]
claims.experts: No published human trial measured endotoxin after eating the salad.[2]

claims.claim: Peat-style eating reduces water retention and puffiness.
claims.believers: Looksmax.org members discuss Peat's views on sodium and water retention for a leaner look.[4]
claims.experts: No published studies were found testing Peat's protocol for facial puffiness.

quick.overview:
The raw carrot salad is a shredded carrot with oil, vinegar and salt, eaten daily by followers of Ray Peat's bioenergetic diet.

People use it hoping for clearer skin, less bloating and a leaner look, and many simply enjoy it as an inexpensive side dish.
quick.mechanism: Followers say carrot fibre helps carry endotoxin and excess estrogen out of the gut, which they link to better skin and body composition. Carrots also supply fibre and carotenoids that can warm skin tone.
quick.risks: Generally a low-risk food. Large amounts of carotenoids may tint the skin orange, and raw fibre can cause gas in some people. No clinical trial has tested the protocol.
